payload.throughline: Conserve volume flow first, then account for pressure, speed, and height under an explicitly idealized flow model.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: A steady incompressible fluid enters a narrower section of one unbranched tube. No leak occurs. What happens to average speed? This is low stakes; it neither selects a route nor establishes mastery.
Goal: Use Q = Av for steady incompressible flow in serial and branched tubes, including area changes derived from radius or diameter.
Bridge: Conservation links what enters and leaves a control region. For an incompressible fluid with steady flow and no leak, the volume crossing each section per unit time must balance.
Volume flow rate is Q = Av, where A is cross-sectional area and v is average flow speed through that section. In one unbranched steady incompressible tube, A1v1 = A2v2.
Area scales with radius squared: A = πr². Halving radius produces one-fourth the area, so speed must become four times as large to preserve the same Q in a serial tube.
At a branch, conservation applies to total flow: Qparent = Qbranch 1 + Qbranch 2 + … . Speeds in the branches depend on both how total Q divides and each branch area.
These conclusions require the stated idealization: steady flow, effectively incompressible fluid, and no accumulation or leakage from the analyzed junction.

Imagine equal-volume packets crossing each section during the same second. A narrower serial section must move packets faster; a branch divides the packet stream so the outgoing rates add to the incoming rate.

A tube radius falls from 2 cm to 1 cm. I compare areas, not radii: the new area is one-fourth. With the same serial flow rate, speed is four times larger. A factor of two would incorrectly treat radius as area.
A parent vessel carries 12 mL/s and divides into three identical branches with equal flow. Each branch carries 4 mL/s.
If each branch area is 2 mm², each branch speed is Q/A after unit alignment. I do not set each branch speed from parent area alone.

Boundary: continuity conserves total volume flow, not speed. Speed need not be equal across sections, and a parent flow rate is not copied into every branch. Radius ratios must be squared before using them as area ratios.

Starting check: Along one ideal streamline at equal height, speed is greater at Point B than Point A. How does static pressure compare? This is low stakes; it neither selects a route nor establishes mastery.
Goal: Relate static pressure, flow speed, and height along an idealized streamline using Bernoulli’s energy balance.
Bridge: Continuity constrains flow rate. Bernoulli adds an energy-per-volume ledger that trades among static pressure, kinetic contribution, and gravitational contribution.
For steady, incompressible, nonviscous flow along a streamline with no added shaft work, P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant.
At equal height, a faster section has a larger kinetic term and therefore a lower static-pressure term under the ideal model.
If speed remains the same while height increases, static pressure decreases by ρgΔh. If pressure remains the same while height increases, speed must decrease.
Bernoulli conclusions do not automatically apply across unrelated streamlines, across pumps or turbines, or where viscous losses are material. State the idealization before using the tradeoff.
Use three energy-density accounts—pressure, motion, and height. Hold their sum constant only after checking ideal-flow conditions and that the points lie on the modeled streamline.

Two points are at the same height, and continuity shows Point 2 is faster. In the Bernoulli ledger, the kinetic term rises at Point 2, so static pressure must fall. I do not say total pressure energy disappears; it changes form.
Water moves from a wide section at 2 m/s to a narrow section at 4 m/s at equal height. The kinetic term increases by ½ρ(4² − 2²), so P2 is lower by that amount under the ideal model.
I rule out using hydrostatic pressure alone because the fluid is moving and the speed changes.

Starting check: In a horizontal ideal Venturi tube, how do speed and static pressure at the narrow throat compare with upstream? This is low stakes; it neither selects a route nor establishes mastery.
Goal: Use constriction and stagnation pressure measurements to infer speed and static-pressure behavior in idealized Venturi and pitot arrangements.
Bridge: Continuity and Bernoulli become measurement tools when geometry creates a speed change or an opening brings flow to rest. The measured pressure difference reveals the exchanged kinetic term.

In a horizontal Venturi constriction, continuity predicts higher speed in the narrow throat. Bernoulli then predicts lower static pressure there. The upstream-to-throat pressure difference can be used to infer flow speed when geometry and density are known.

A pitot opening facing the flow brings fluid locally to a stagnation point where v = 0. At the same height in the ideal model, stagnation pressure exceeds static pressure by the dynamic pressure: ΔP = ½ρv².
Pitot speed follows v = √(2ΔP/ρ). Venturi and pitot devices use different pressure comparisons: Venturi compares two flowing sections; pitot compares stagnation and static pressure.
A larger stagnation-minus-static pressure difference implies greater speed for the same density. Real measurements require calibration and loss corrections beyond this idealized scope.

Use two measurement stories: squeeze the stream to exchange static pressure for speed in a Venturi, or stop a tiny portion of the stream to convert kinetic contribution into stagnation pressure in a pitot tube.

A pitot record gives stagnation pressure 450 Pa above static pressure in air. I set ΔP = ½ρv² and solve for v. I do not treat the 450 Pa as a Venturi throat pressure drop unless the diagram shows two flowing sections.
For water with ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and pitot ΔP = 2000 Pa, v = √(2×2000/1000) = 2 m/s.
At a horizontal Venturi throat, speed is greater and static pressure lower than upstream. The pressure difference is consistent with the kinetic-term increase, not with pressure disappearing.

Boundary: static pressure and stagnation pressure are not interchangeable. Venturi throat pressure falls while flow remains moving; pitot stagnation pressure rises where the sampled streamline is brought locally to rest.
